item.title: ServiceNow AI Platform Pre-Auth RCE Is Being Exploited (CVE-2026-6875)
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Attackers are hitting an unauthenticated code-execution flaw in ServiceNow's AI Platform within days of the patch, using a sandbox escape that reaches the platform's Rhino engine.
item.content:encoded:
A pre-authentication flaw in ServiceNow's AI Platform went from patch to in-the-wild exploitation in a matter of days, and the way in runs through an endpoint almost nobody thinks about.

CVE-2026-6875 is a sandbox escape. ServiceNow restricts what user-supplied scripts can do, but this bug carves a path from that restricted execution to a full code-execution primitive. Public research points to /assessment_thanks.do as a pre-auth sink that accepts attacker-controlled input, and a successful escape reaches ServiceNow's Rhino scripting engine. From there an attacker can read data straight out of tables, create administrator accounts, and run shell commands on configured proxy servers. Searchlight Cyber reported the issue to ServiceNow on April 1.

The exploitation is real, not theoretical. Defused observed in-the-wild attempts against the same pre-auth endpoint documented in the public write-up, though the attacks use a different escape route than the one researchers published. That detail matters. It means more than one working technique exists for the same door.

ServiceNow is where a lot of large organizations run their actual operations: tickets, approvals, HR records, IT workflows. Unauthenticated code execution on that tier is close to a keys-to-the-kingdom problem, and the data it exposes tends to be exactly the stuff you don't want walking out.

ServiceNow has pushed updates to hosted instances and shipped patches to self-hosted customers and partners. If you run your own instance, treat this as patch-now, not patch-this-sprint. If you're on a hosted instance, confirm the update landed rather than assuming it did.

item.title: Ransomware Halts Coca-Cola's Fairlife US Milk Production
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Coca-Cola disclosed a ransomware attack that suspended US production at its Fairlife dairy subsidiary, and the Anubis group claims it stole a terabyte of data.
item.content:encoded:
Coca-Cola's ultra-filtered milk brand stopped rolling off US production lines this month, and not because of a supply problem. Ransomware got into the systems that run the plants.

Coca-Cola disclosed the incident in an SEC 8-K filing on July 16, saying attackers reached a portion of Fairlife's systems, including production-related ones, by way of a third party. US production was temporarily suspended. Canadian operations kept running, and the company says product quality and safety were not affected.

On July 20 a ransomware crew called Anubis listed Coca-Cola and Fairlife on its leak site, then publicly claimed the attack over the following days. Anubis says it encrypted Fairlife's Nutanix systems and walked off with roughly a terabyte of confidential data. Coca-Cola, for its part, activated incident response and business continuity plans, brought in outside cybersecurity advisors, and notified law enforcement.

Anubis is worth knowing by name. Researchers have documented a wiper mode in its toolkit capable of permanently deleting files, which turns a recoverable incident into an irreversible one. The group also disables volume shadow copies and interferes with security processes before encryption, so the usual answer of "we'll just restore from backup" gets harder if the operators did their homework.

The pattern here should bother anyone running a plant floor. This wasn't a stolen spreadsheet. It was an attack that reached the systems tied to physical production and stopped the line. Food and manufacturing operators have spent years treating OT as separate and safer than IT. Incidents like this keep proving that the wall between the two is thinner than the org chart suggests.

item.title: Working GitLab RCE Exploit Published for a Flaw With No CVE
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A researcher released code that runs commands as git on unpatched self-managed GitLab, exploiting a June fix that GitLab quietly filed under bug fixes with no CVE.
item.content:encoded:
The exploit works on any self-managed GitLab that skipped a June update. There's no CVE for it, no CVSS score, and GitLab filed the fix under "bug fixes."

On July 24, researchers at depthfirst published working exploit code for a flaw GitLab had already patched six weeks earlier, on June 10. Run against a self-managed 18.11.3 server that never took the update, it executes commands as the git user. The underlying chain runs through Oj, a fast native C JSON parser used across a lot of Ruby applications, GitLab included. depthfirst's Yuhang Wu found it by pointing an automated analysis system at the parser.

GitLab moved quickly on the fix itself. The chain was reported June 5, confirmed June 8, and patched June 10 across the 19.0.2, 18.11.5, and 18.10.8 releases.

Here's the part that should annoy defenders. GitLab didn't file it as a security fix. A review by The Hacker News found the Oj 3.17.3 bump listed under bug fixes in the June 10 notes, not in the security-fix table. No CVE, no CVSS, no mention of the exploit chain. If you triage patches by severity rating, this one had no rating to triage by. It reads like routine maintenance right up until someone hands you working exploit code.

The takeaway is simple and a little uncomfortable: a version bump in a changelog isn't the same as a heads-up, and "we shipped the fix" and "we told you it mattered" are two different things. If you run self-managed GitLab, get current now. And if you assume your vulnerability scanner catches everything worth catching, remember that a fix with no CVE is invisible to most of them.

item.title: AMD's EPYC Venice Puts 256 Zen 6 Cores on TSMC's 2nm Node
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: AMD launched its sixth-gen EPYC server chips at Advancing AI 2026, the first x86 server CPU to reach volume production on TSMC's 2nm gate-all-around process.
item.content:encoded:
Two hundred fifty-six cores in one socket, on a 2nm process that wasn't in any shipping server chip until this week.

AMD introduced EPYC Venice at its Advancing AI 2026 event in San Francisco on July 22. It's the sixth-generation EPYC line, built on the Zen 6 architecture, and the first x86 server CPU to reach volume production on TSMC's 2nm N2 node. That node switch is the real headline. N2 brings gate-all-around nanosheet transistors, replacing the FinFET design that has been the industry standard since 2011.

The core math changed too. Venice uses eight core complex dies with 32 cores each, instead of the previous generation's arrangement, and the flagship lands at 256 cores and 512 threads in a single socket with 1,024 MB of L3 cache and around 203 billion transistors. The platform moves to a new SP7 socket with 16 memory channels, up to 1.6 TB/s of bandwidth, and PCIe Gen 6, which doubles per-lane bandwidth for shoveling data between CPUs and GPUs.

AMD is claiming a 70% performance uplift over the prior generation alongside the 33% jump in core count. Treat the 70% as a vendor number until independent benchmarks land, because that figure always depends on which workload you pick. But the structural story stands on its own. More cores, more memory bandwidth, and a faster path to the GPUs is exactly the shape of chip that AI data centers are starving for.

The interesting subplot is the process node. Being first to volume on N2 is a bet as much as an achievement, and it puts AMD ahead of where a lot of people expected 2nm server silicon to actually ship. If the yields hold, that lead is worth more than the core count.

item.title: Google Is Spending on AI Faster Than the Cash Comes In
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Alphabet beat on Q2 revenue but raised its 2026 capital spending to as much as $205 billion, pushing free cash flow negative and sinking the stock.
item.content:encoded:
Google is making more money than ever and spending it faster than it comes in.

Alphabet reported second-quarter revenue of about $119.8 billion, up 24% from a year earlier and ahead of the roughly $117 billion analysts expected. The stock fell anyway. Investors weren't reacting to the beat. They were reacting to the bill.

The company raised its full-year 2026 capital spending guidance to a range of $195 to $205 billion, up from $180 to $190 billion. Quarterly capex hit $44.9 billion, roughly double the year-ago figure. Management said about 60% of the spend goes to servers and the rest to data centers and networking gear. All of that pushed free cash flow into negative territory, which for a business that mints cash the way Google's search engine does is a genuinely unusual sentence to write.

This is the AI infrastructure bet stated in dollars. Alphabet is wagering that demand for AI compute, both for its own products and for cloud customers, will justify building capacity ahead of the revenue. Cloud growth is real and strong, which is the part of the argument that holds up. The part investors are chewing on is the timing: you're spending certain money now against demand you're forecasting later.

The question worth sitting with isn't whether AI matters. It's what return actually justifies going cash-flow negative to chase it, and how long shareholders stay patient while the answer takes shape.

item.title: Meta's New Seller App Lets AI Write Your Marketplace Listings
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Meta launched Seller, a standalone iOS app for Facebook Marketplace where Meta AI drafts the title, description, price, and shipping label from a photo.
item.content:encoded:
Meta wants selling on Facebook Marketplace to feel like taking a photo and walking away.

On July 24, Facebook head Tom Alison introduced Seller, a standalone iOS app built around Marketplace. The pitch is that you upload a photo of whatever you're offloading and Meta AI drafts the rest: title, description, suggested price, and category. The listing that used to take a few minutes of typing becomes a review-and-post. The app is free, aimed at US power sellers 18 and up, and ships with a unified inbox, inventory management, and performance data on views, clicks, and sold items. An Android version is in the works.

Pulling Marketplace into its own app is a notable move on its own. Marketplace listings run to roughly 430 million a month, so treating selling as a distinct behavior worth its own front door rather than a tab buried in the blue app makes sense. The AI layer is the part that will make or break it in practice.

The friction Meta is removing is real. Writing a decent listing is tedious, and plenty of good items never get posted because the seller couldn't be bothered. But letting the model set the price is where trust gets tested. Sellers know what their stuff is worth to them, and an AI suggestion that's off in either direction is the kind of thing that sends people right back to typing it themselves. The description-and-category automation is the easy win. The pricing is the bet.

item.title: Kimi K3 Agents Found Redis Zero-Days and Wrote the Exploit in Minutes
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Moonshot's Kimi K3 agents surfaced authenticated RCE bugs in stock Redis builds, and the project shipped seven emergency releases on July 23.
item.content:encoded:
Twenty-seven minutes. That's how long a Kimi K3 agent reportedly needed to turn a fresh Redis flaw into a working remote code execution exploit, according to the researcher who ran it.

The claim comes from Chaofan Shou, who said on X that Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 agents surfaced 19 Redis zero-days in roughly 90 minutes across the stock builds of Redis 6.2.22, 7.4.9, 8.6.4, and 8.8.0. A follow-up run, he said, produced a full exploit for 8.8.0 in under half an hour. Those numbers are self-reported, and neither the count nor the degree of autonomy has been independently verified.

Here's what isn't in dispute. Redis shipped seven security releases on July 23 after authenticated RCE proof-of-concepts went public. The headline bug, CVE-2026-23631, is a Lua use-after-free that an authenticated user can trigger through the master-replica synchronization path on replicas with replica-read-only disabled. It carries a moderate CVSS of 6.1, which undersells how the published chain actually behaves.

The exploit stitches two problems together: a shared-ownership bug in the Redis Streams consumer-group path, where a corrupt RDB object makes two consumers point at the same pending-entry record so removing both frees it twice, and a separate heap overflow in the bundled RedisBloom TDigest module. The public script walks that double-free into arbitrary memory access and, eventually, a call to system(). Redis confirmed the flaws and the fixes. It did not confirm how the bugs were found.

The AI angle deserves the skepticism the AI beat rarely gets. "An agent found it" is doing a lot of marketing work in the retelling, and a self-reported 27-minute exploit is not a benchmark anyone can reproduce yet. But strip the theater and something real is left: the patched flaws exist, the PoCs run, and the turnaround from disclosure to weaponized code was short enough that Redis pushed an emergency batch on a Thursday. Whether a human or a model did the finding, the defensive clock is the same.

No in-the-wild exploitation has been reported as of July 24. Upgrade to the patched Redis builds, and if you run replicas with replica-read-only turned off, treat that as the priority.

item.title: CISA Says Russian Hackers Read NATO Email for a Year via Zimbra Bug
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A joint CISA and NSA advisory ties the Russia-aligned LAUNDRY BEAR group to a zero-click Zimbra flaw used to steal mail and 2FA codes since 2025.
item.content:encoded:
Russian intelligence spent the better part of a year reading other people's email, and the victims never had to click anything to let them in.

CISA, the NSA, and more than two dozen partner agencies issued a joint advisory on July 23 tying a Russia-aligned espionage group to active exploitation of a Zimbra webmail flaw. The group is tracked as LAUNDRY BEAR, also filed under TA488 and Void Blizzard. The agencies assess it has been harvesting mail and two-factor codes since at least July 2025.

The bug is CVE-2025-66376, a stored cross-site scripting flaw in Zimbra's webmail client that Zimbra fixed on November 6, 2025. Exploitation started months before the patch. The root cause is unglamorous: Zimbra didn't properly sanitize CSS @import directives inside email content, which let attacker-controlled script ride in on a message.

What makes this one nasty is that viewing the email is the whole attack. No link, no attachment, no second step. The script runs silently in the victim's browser session and starts pulling session tokens, backup 2FA codes, browser-saved passwords, and the contents of the mailbox going back 90 days. The stolen data leaves over a mix of DNS and HTTPS, which helps it blend into normal traffic.

The target list reads like a Russian collection wishlist: Ukrainian government bodies, US government and defense organizations, nuclear facilities, and scientific institutions across Europe. Stealing backup 2FA codes is the tell. This wasn't smash-and-grab; it was built to survive password resets and keep access alive.

If you run on-prem Zimbra and haven't applied the November fix, assume compromise rather than exposure, and rotate credentials and 2FA seeds for anyone whose mailbox was reachable. A patch stops the bleeding. It doesn't evict someone who has been inside since last summer.

item.title: RefluXFS Flaw Lets Local Users Gain Root on XFS Linux Systems
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Qualys disclosed a race condition in the Linux kernel's XFS copy-on-write path that hands unprivileged local users persistent root.
item.content:encoded:
A local user on an XFS filesystem can now become root by racing the kernel against itself, and the exploit leaves almost nothing behind.

Qualys's Threat Research Unit published RefluXFS on July 22, tracked as CVE-2026-64600. It's a race condition in the Linux kernel's XFS copy-on-write path, and it turns an unprivileged local account into full host root.

The flaw lives in how XFS handles reflinked files. When two O_DIRECT writes hit the same reflinked file at once, the kernel can briefly drop the inode lock while it waits for transaction log space. In that window, the second writer finishes its own remap and changes the block's reference state. The first writer wakes up, trusts metadata that's now stale, and writes straight to the original block instead of a private copy. The result is that an unprivileged process can overwrite the on-disk contents of any file it can read.

This isn't a memory-corruption bug, and that's what makes it interesting. There's no heap grooming, no bypass of the usual kernel hardening. It corrupts data on disk directly, so the root you get persists across reboots and leaves the kind of thin forensic trail that makes incident response miserable.

Three conditions have to line up: a kernel at v4.11 or later without the patch, an XFS volume with reflink=1 in its superblock, and a directory a normal user can write to alongside a file worth overwriting. That combination is common on modern server distributions where XFS with reflinks is the default. No in-the-wild use has been reported.

Patch the kernel. If you can't reboot right away, the practical first step is knowing which of your boxes actually run XFS with reflinks, because that's the population that matters.

item.title: Hackers Sat in South Korea's Diplomat Training System for 10 Months
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Seoul disclosed a ten-month intrusion into the National Diplomatic Academy that exposed personal data on thousands of current and former diplomats.
item.content:encoded:
For ten months, someone had a quiet seat inside the system South Korea uses to train its diplomats, and nobody in Seoul noticed.

The Foreign Ministry disclosed this week that attackers breached the National Diplomatic Academy's online education platform and pulled personal data on current and former ministry staff, including diplomats posted overseas. The intrusion ran from April 2025 until February 2026, when an outside government body flagged abnormal access and the ministry took the platform offline the same day.

The official count is at least 6,000 people affected, including roughly 350 attaches currently stationed abroad. Korean media put the real number closer to 10,000. The exposed data covers IDs, names, email addresses, and hashed passwords. The ministry says national ID numbers, mobile numbers, photos, and home addresses were not in the haul.

The part worth sitting with is the timeline. Seoul recognized the breach in February and said nothing publicly until July, citing the sensitivity of diplomatic and security matters. Five months of silence is a long time to leave several hundred officials abroad unaware that their credentials might be in a hostile hand.

A training-academy portal sounds like a soft target, and it was, but the payoff was a roster of the country's diplomatic corps. Hashed passwords buy some time depending on the algorithm, not immunity. Anyone in that dataset should assume their login is known and move accordingly.

item.title: AMD and Cerebras Team Up to Split AI Inference Across Their Chips
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A new deal divides inference workloads between AMD and Cerebras hardware, with AMD's Helios systems heading into Cerebras Cloud this year.
item.content:encoded:
AMD and Cerebras are splitting a single AI inference job across two very different chips, and betting the seam between them is where the speed hides.

The two companies announced a technical partnership on July 23 for what they call a disaggregated inference system. AMD's Helios rackscale hardware handles the heavy front end, processing prompts and long context, while Cerebras's Wafer-Scale Engine takes over the low-latency decoding and token generation. The idea is to let each chip do the part it's best at instead of forcing one design to cover the whole pipeline.

AMD and Cerebras say the combined setup can deliver up to 5x higher tokens per second per watt than a Cerebras-only configuration, based on their own July modeling. That's a vendor projection, not a measured result, so treat it as a target rather than a spec. The joint solution is slated to land through Cerebras Cloud in the second half of the year, with Cerebras deploying Helios systems in its own data centers.

The timing says as much as the tech. This lands during a rough stretch for chip stocks, with the semiconductor sector down more than 20% from its June peak, and it follows AMD's recent inference deal with Anthropic. AMD shares still slipped a few percent on the news. The market's question right now isn't whether inference demand is real; it's whether current valuations already assumed all of it.

Disaggregated inference is a genuinely interesting bet. The lead may not belong to whoever builds the biggest single chip, but to whoever divides the work most cleverly. The back half of the year will show whether customers actually want to buy their inference in two pieces.

item.title: Transformer-Chip Startup Etched Raises $300M at a $10.3B Valuation
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Etched closed a $300 million Series C at a $10.3 billion valuation for its Sohu ASICs built to run only transformer models.
item.content:encoded:
A chip that runs exactly one kind of AI model just raised $300 million, and the investors betting on it think that narrowness is the point.

Etched closed a $300 million Series C at a $10.3 billion valuation, led by Sequoia with Andreessen Horowitz, Jane Street, Argo, and SK Hynix joining. Reuters noted it's the highest valuation on any Series C the firm has led. The figure roughly doubled from the company's reported $5 billion valuation earlier this year.

Etched's pitch is a deliberate gamble. Its Sohu chip hardcodes the transformer architecture directly into silicon, trading the flexibility of a general-purpose GPU for raw efficiency on the one model shape that dominates AI right now. If transformers stay on top, Sohu runs them faster and cheaper than Nvidia's hardware. If the field moves to something else, a chip that only speaks transformer becomes a very expensive paperweight.

The founders Gavin Uberti, Robert Wachen, and Chris Zhu started the company as Harvard dropouts in 2022. Etched says it's holding around $1 billion in contracts with racks shipping this summer, which is the detail that separates this round from pure story-stock territory.

The raise fits a broader pattern this year, where roughly 60% of global startup funding has flowed into billion-dollar-plus rounds concentrated in AI and infrastructure. Specialized inference silicon is now a crowded, well-funded fight. Etched picked the boldest position in it, and just got the capital to find out if it's right.

item.title: Tesla Delivered a Record Quarter and Made Less Money Doing It
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Tesla beat on revenue with 480,126 deliveries but missed profit estimates as spending on AI and robotics pushed operating income down 57%.
item.content:encoded:
Tesla delivered a record 480,126 vehicles in the second quarter, up 25% from a year ago and well past the roughly 407,000 analysts expected. Revenue hit $28.24 billion. And the stock fell about 4% after hours anyway.

The problem was the bottom line. Adjusted earnings came in at 33 cents a share against a consensus closer to 49, and operating profit fell 57% year over year even as sales rose. Operating expenses jumped 47% to $4.35 billion, most of it going into AI infrastructure and R&D rather than the car business.

Tesla also burned cash, posting a free-cash-flow deficit of about $1.09 billion after a surplus in the prior quarter.

The split screen is the whole story. Tesla is selling more cars than ever, at lower margins, while pouring the proceeds into the AI and robotics bets Elon Musk keeps telling investors are the real company. Whether that reads as visionary reinvestment or a car maker quietly getting less profitable depends entirely on whether the robots show up.

For now, the market is being asked to pay a technology multiple for a company whose actual product got cheaper to sell this quarter. That's a bet, and Q2 didn't make it an easier one to hold.

item.title: Alphabet Beat Everything and Fell 6% on One Number: Capex
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Alphabet raised 2026 capital spending guidance to as much as $205 billion, spooking investors even as cloud revenue grew 82%.
item.content:encoded:
Alphabet beat on revenue, beat on profit, grew its cloud business 82% in a single year, and watched its stock drop more than 6%. The reason was one line on the guidance page. The company now expects to spend between $195 and $205 billion on capital expenditure this year, up from the $180 to $190 billion it guided a quarter ago.

The quarter itself was enormous. Revenue hit $119.8 billion against expectations near $116.9 billion, earnings came in at $9.11 a share, and Google Cloud jumped to $24.77 billion in revenue, up 82% year over year as AI workloads filled capacity as fast as Alphabet could build it.

Google spent $44.9 billion on infrastructure in the quarter alone, more than double a year ago.

This is the tension sitting under every hyperscaler's earnings right now. Cloud demand is real and the growth is real, but the spend required to serve it is climbing faster than the revenue it produces, and Alphabet told investors 2027 capex will rise significantly on top of this year's. The market's 6% haircut wasn't a vote against AI. It was a question about when the bill stops growing faster than the return.

For everyone downstream of these decisions, from chip suppliers to power utilities to the startups renting this capacity, the message is that the buildout isn't slowing. Alphabet just told the market it plans to spend more, sooner, and dared it to complain.

item.title: Origin Energy Confirms Breach; Attacker Claims 2 Million Customer Records
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Australia's Origin Energy says an unknown attacker stole customer data including names, dates of birth, and partial card and bank details.
item.content:encoded:
Origin Energy, one of Australia's largest power and gas retailers, confirmed on July 23 that an unknown attacker got into its systems and made off with customer data. The company has about 4.8 million customers and is still working out how many were caught in the breach. A threat actor claiming responsibility says the haul covers 2 million of them.

The exposed fields are the usual identity-theft starter kit: name, address, date of birth, phone number, and account details. More concerning is what came with it. For some customers the data includes the last four digits of a credit card or the last three of a bank account.

That's not enough to drain an account on its own, but it's plenty to make a phishing call or a fake 'Origin billing' text sound convincing.

Origin says it has notified the Australian Federal Police, the Australian Cyber Security Centre, and the national privacy regulator, and is contacting affected customers directly through a dedicated support portal. It hasn't named the attacker or explained how the intrusion happened.

Australia has spent the past few years as a case study in large-scale consumer breaches, from Optus to Medibank, and the pattern holds here: a big retailer, a huge customer base, and a slow drip of detail while the company maps the blast radius. Expect the confirmed-impact number to move as the investigation runs.

If you're an Origin customer, the practical move is boring and effective. Assume your contact details are out, and be skeptical of any call or message that references your Origin account and asks you to verify anything.

item.title: Fake Claude Installer Rode a Real claude.ai Link to Push SectopRAT
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Huntress says the FakeAgent campaign used Bing ads and a public Claude Artifact hosted on claude.ai to deliver SectopRAT to at least 29 organizations.
item.content:encoded:
The link pointed at claude.ai. The domain was legitimate, the page looked like exactly what someone searching Bing for 'Claude Desktop' expected, and the file behind the download button was SectopRAT.

Researchers at Huntress, who named the campaign FakeAgent, say attackers bought sponsored Bing ads that led to a public Claude Artifact built to imitate Anthropic's official desktop installer. Because Artifacts are hosted on the real claude.ai domain, the whole thing sailed past the mental check most people run before clicking a download. Hitting the button kicked off a redirect chain through attacker-controlled domains that ended in a malicious ClaudeDesktop.exe.

The artifact was downloaded roughly 7,100 times before Anthropic pulled it, and Huntress counted at least 29 organizations compromised over two days, July 21 and 22.

SectopRAT, also tracked as ArechClient2, has been around since 2019. It's an information stealer with hidden-VNC capability, meaning an operator can quietly drive an infected machine in real time while lifting saved passwords, browser cookies, card numbers, and credentials from messaging and FTP clients. One detail stands out: the malware pulls its command-and-control address out of Ethereum transactions on the BNB Smart Chain, a technique called EtherHiding that makes the C2 nearly impossible to take down.

The uncomfortable part isn't the malware, which is years old and well understood. It's the delivery. A trusted platform that lets anyone publish content on its primary domain becomes a laundering service for exactly this kind of lure, and 'check the URL before you click' training does nothing when the URL is genuinely correct.

Download desktop software from the vendor's own documented link, not from a search ad, and treat any 'official app' that arrives through a sponsored result as suspect until proven otherwise. The domain being real doesn't mean the file is.

item.title: Clop Turns a PTC Windchill Flaw Into Its Latest Mass Data-Theft Campaign
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The Clop gang is exploiting CVE-2026-12569 to drop web shells on internet-exposed Windchill and FlexPLM servers and steal manufacturers' product data.
item.content:encoded:
Clop is back to doing the thing it does best: find one enterprise application with a critical bug, then quietly empty out everyone running it. This time the target is PTC's Windchill and FlexPLM, the product lifecycle management platforms manufacturers use to store design files, bills of materials, and the guts of how their products get built.

The gang is exploiting CVE-2026-12569, a critical deserialization flaw rated 9.3 that lets an unauthenticated attacker run code on an internet-exposed Windchill or FlexPLM server. Clop's operators drop JSP web shells onto compromised instances and use them to exfiltrate whatever product data is sitting there. No encryption, no locked files. Just theft and an extortion note.

This is the same playbook Clop ran against MOVEit and every other mass-exploitation campaign it's built its name on. Steal at scale, list victims on a leak site, and let the threat of publication do the negotiating.

PTC started shipping patches for the flaw on June 17 and warned customers of heightened threat activity on June 26. CISA added CVE-2026-12569 to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and gave federal agencies three days to patch or pull the systems offline. If you run Windchill or FlexPLM with any internet exposure, treat it as compromised until you've hunted for JSP web shells and confirmed the June fix is applied.

PLM data is exactly the kind of thing that never shows up in a credit-monitoring letter but absolutely shows up in a competitor's hands.

The patch has been out for over a month. The organizations getting hit now are the ones that assumed a PLM server was too obscure to be a target. Clop's entire business model is proving that assumption wrong.

item.title: Intel Posts Fastest Growth Since 2011 as 18A Foundry Finally Delivers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Intel's Q2 revenue hit $16.1B on a 25% jump, with foundry and its 18A node beating targets and adjusted EPS coming in at double estimates.
item.content:encoded:
Intel's second quarter came in at $16.1 billion in revenue, up 25% from a year earlier. That's the company's fastest growth in more than 15 years, and it blew past the roughly $14.4 billion Wall Street had penciled in. Shares jumped more than 13% after hours.

The number that actually matters for Intel's long game is the foundry line. Intel Foundry pulled in $5.8 billion, up 31%, and CFO David Zinsner credited the 18A process node for the jump. He said 18A output ran about 25% above target and climbed more than 50% from the prior quarter. After years of Intel insisting its manufacturing comeback was one node away, this is the first quarter where the numbers back the story.

Data Center and AI was the other bright spot. That segment topped $6.3 billion, up 59% from a year ago and 24% quarter over quarter, as buyers kept absorbing anything that could sit next to a GPU. Gross margin recovered to 42%, a world away from the 2.5% Intel scraped together in the same quarter last year when write-downs gutted the line.

Adjusted earnings landed at 42 cents a share, roughly double what analysts modeled.

There's a catch, and Zinsner named it himself: supply, not demand, is now the constraint. Intel is selling everything 18A can make and still can't make enough. That's a far better problem than the one Intel had two years ago, but it caps how fast the recovery can compound and hands rivals like TSMC a window while Intel races to add capacity.

For a company that spent the back half of the last decade as the cautionary tale of American chipmaking, a quarter like this changes the conversation. The question now isn't whether 18A works. It's whether Intel can build enough of it before the AI buildout finds another supplier.

item.title: Cisco's Security Certs Get an AI and Zero-Trust Rewrite on August 27
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Cisco is updating the 350-701 SCOR exam to v2.0 and refreshing its CCNP and CCIE Security tracks with AI security and SASE content, with the last day to test on the old versions being August 26.
item.content:encoded:
If you've been sitting on a half-finished CCNP Security, this is your notice to either finish it or plan to relearn part of it. Cisco is rolling the 350-701 SCOR core exam from v1.1 to v2.0 on August 27, and it's retiring three legacy exams the same day.

The last day to test on the current versions is August 26. Miss that window and you're taking the new blueprint. This is part of the broader overhaul Cisco kicked off earlier in the year, the biggest shake-up to its certification program in over a decade, and the security track is where the changes bite hardest.

The content shift tracks where enterprise security work has actually gone. The refreshed SCOR exam, and the CCIE Security written that shares its blueprint, adds AI and LLM security topics, including prompt injection and data poisoning, the kind of attacks that didn't exist as exam objectives a couple of years ago. Zero Trust, SSE, and SASE move to the center, largely displacing the traditional site-to-site VPN material that used to anchor this exam. The concentration exams pick up cloud-native security models and AI-assisted threat detection.

None of this is padding. Prompt injection against an internal LLM tool and an over-trusted service mesh are real things security engineers are being asked about now, and a cert that still tested you mostly on IPsec tunnels would be teaching to a job that's fading.

Practical advice if you're mid-study: figure out honestly whether you can be ready by August 26. If yes, sit v1.1 while your prep still matches the exam. If not, don't cram against a moving target. Pivot now to v2.0 materials, lean into the Zero Trust and AI-security sections, and treat the extra scope as the part of the job you were going to have to learn anyway.

item.title: Amazon's In-House Chips Are Quietly a $20 Billion Business
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Between Trainium, Graviton, and Nitro, Amazon's custom silicon is running at roughly $20 billion a year and Amazon is reportedly weighing selling the AI chips to outside customers.
item.content:encoded:
Ask who's challenging Nvidia and the usual answers are AMD and a handful of startups. The more interesting answer is a company most people think of as a bookstore and a cloud.

Amazon's custom silicon effort, spanning its Trainium AI accelerators, Graviton server CPUs, and Nitro networking chips, is now running at an annualized rate of about $20 billion, with all three lines growing at triple-digit percentages year over year. That figure alone would rank the operation among the larger chip businesses on the planet, and it's mostly invisible because nearly all of it is consumed inside AWS rather than sold on a shelf.

The demand behind Trainium in particular is real money, not slideware. CEO Andy Jassy has pointed to roughly $225 billion in Trainium commitments, with Anthropic, OpenAI, and Uber among the names driving it. Trainium2 is largely sold out. Trainium3, which started shipping earlier this year, is nearly fully subscribed, and pre-reservations for Trainium4 are already substantial ahead of a broad rollout that's still more than a year out.

What makes this a story now rather than a footnote is a shift in posture. Amazon is reportedly weighing whether to sell Trainium to third parties directly, which would put it in head-to-head competition with Nvidia instead of merely reducing its own dependence on Nvidia's supply. That's a different game, and a harder one, because selling chips to strangers means supporting a software stack, courting outside developers, and answering to customers who can walk.

The subtext under all of it is the same pressure squeezing every hyperscaler: GPUs are expensive and scarce, and owning the silicon is the only durable way to control the cost of AI at scale. Amazon has been at this longer than most, and the run-rate number is the receipt.

Whether it graduates from an internal cost-saver into an actual merchant chip vendor is the question worth watching. Building a great accelerator is one thing. Getting anyone outside your own data centers to bet a training run on it is another.

item.title: Apple Turns to Klarna to Lease You an iPhone
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Apple's new Apple Upgrade program, launching July 28 with Klarna financing, lets US buyers lease iPhones, iPads, Macs, and Watches on fixed monthly payments.
item.content:encoded:
Apple is about to stop selling you a phone and start renting you one. On July 28 it launches Apple Upgrade, a lease-to-own program backed by the buy-now-pay-later lender Klarna, available to US customers in Apple Stores and online.

The mechanics are straightforward. You pass a light credit check, then pay a fixed amount each month over a set term: 24 months for iPhones and Apple Watches, 36 months for Macs and iPads. At the end you pick one of three doors. Return the device, pay a fee to jump early to a newer model, or pay off the balance and keep the hardware for good.

This isn't entirely new territory for Apple. It's had an iPhone Upgrade Program for years, and Apple Upgrade largely absorbs and replaces it. What's changed is the scope, now spanning the full hardware lineup, and the partner. Handing the financing to Klarna rather than running it in-house tells you Apple wants the leasing volume without carrying all the consumer credit risk itself.

The why is not subtle. Device prices have crept up, people are holding their phones longer, and per Bloomberg's reporting the program is aimed squarely at softening demand. Spreading a $1,200 phone across 24 payments makes the sticker easier to swallow and, not coincidentally, nudges buyers toward an upgrade cadence that a four-year-old iPhone doesn't encourage.

For the customer the math is worth doing before you sign. Leasing lowers the monthly hit but you don't own anything until the final payment, and pairing a hardware lease with a BNPL lender is exactly the kind of arrangement that's easy to enter and easy to stop paying attention to. Read the early-upgrade fee closely. That's the lever that keeps you on the treadmill.

item.title: AI-Built Apps Fixed the SQL Injection and Left the Doors Unlocked
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A study that built 28 apps with AI coding agents and then attacked them found 434 confirmed vulnerabilities, and the pattern of what the models got wrong is the interesting part.
item.content:encoded:
Give a coding model a spec and it will write you an app that sanitizes its inputs and reaches for prepared statements on its own. Then it will forget to put a lock on the front door.

That's the shape of a new study from security firm Theori, run through its Xint autonomous pentesting platform. The team built 28 applications using AI coding agents, spread across five models from Anthropic and OpenAI, and generated them three ways: from a written spec, from casual throwaway prompts, and by rewriting an aging PHP codebase. Then they attacked everything they'd built.

The scanners threw off 8,827 raw detections. After collapsing duplicates and actually building proof-of-concept exploits to confirm each one, the count settled at 434 real, exploitable vulnerabilities. Of those, 196 lived in the from-scratch apps. The remaining 238 all came from the single project that rewrote legacy PHP, which is a strong hint that pointing a model at old code inherits old problems and adds new ones.

Here's the twist that matters for anyone leaning on these tools. Classic injection flaws barely showed up. The models had genuinely learned to avoid the bugs that get screenshotted in security talks. What they missed was the unglamorous stuff: the largest single category was resource exhaustion and denial-of-service weaknesses, roughly a fifth of all confirmed findings, mostly missing rate limiting. Right behind it came broken access control (the kind where you change an ID in the URL and see someone else's data), server-side request forgery, directory traversal, and exposed secrets.

None of those are exotic. They're the boring, boilerplate protections a human developer adds because they've been burned before, and a model generating plausible code has no reason to include unless you ask. It writes the feature. It doesn't write the guardrail.

The practical read: AI-assisted code is fine to use and getting better at the flashy vulnerability classes, but it is not producing secure applications by default, and the security debt compounds as the codebase grows. Treat generated code like a fast junior's first draft. It needs the same authorization checks, rate limits, and secrets review you'd demand from anyone else, and skipping that step because 'the AI wrote it' is how 434 of these ended up in a lab instead of production.

item.title: AsyncAPI npm Packages Backdoored to Run Malware the Moment You Import Them
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Attackers hijacked the AsyncAPI generator's release pipeline and shipped credential-stealing code that fires at import time, defeating the usual --ignore-scripts defense.
item.content:encoded:
The defense half the industry reaches for when a package looks sketchy is npm install --ignore-scripts. In this attack it did nothing.

On July 14, three packages in the AsyncAPI generator monorepo were published to npm carrying an obfuscated dropper: @asyncapi/generator@3.3.1, @asyncapi/generator-helpers@1.1.1, and @asyncapi/generator-components@0.7.1. Together the affected @asyncapi packages pull more than 3 million downloads a week. The payload doesn't wait for a postinstall hook. It runs the moment the library is loaded, which is why ignoring install scripts bought nobody any protection.

The way in is the part worth studying. An attacker opened dozens of pull requests against the generator repo, then used that noise to camouflage one, PR #2155, that exploited a GitHub Actions 'pwn request' misconfiguration. That gave them the credentials of the bot account that cuts releases. From there they pushed malicious commits straight to two pre-production branches, next and schema, that had been left unprotected. No human ever reviewed the code that shipped.

Researchers who pulled the payload apart describe it as a descendant of the Miasma remote access trojan, a multi-stage botnet that steals credentials from the developer machine or CI runner that loads the poisoned module. For anyone running the generator in a build pipeline, that means the secrets in that pipeline should be considered exposed.

AsyncAPI moved fast once it was flagged. Every malicious version has been unpublished from the registry, and the latest tag for each package now points at a clean build. If you installed one of those exact versions between July 14 and the takedown, updating isn't enough. Rotate any tokens, keys, or credentials that were present in the environment where the build ran.

The uncomfortable lesson here isn't about AsyncAPI specifically. It's that a project can protect its main branch, require reviews, and still get owned through a forgotten release branch and an over-permissioned CI workflow. The registry is only as trustworthy as the weakest automation behind it.

item.title: Attackers Log In as Admin on Check Point Firewalls via SmartConsole Bug
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: CVE-2026-16232 lets an unauthenticated attacker reach a Check Point management server and take it over with full admin rights, and it's already being exploited.
item.content:encoded:
The box you use to manage your firewalls just became the way in. Check Point confirmed this week that attackers are abusing a flaw in SmartConsole, the client admins use to run Check Point management servers, to authenticate as a full administrator with no password at all.

The bug is CVE-2026-16232, and Check Point rates it 9.1 on the CVSS scale. It's an authentication bypass in the SmartConsole login process: an unauthenticated attacker who can reach the management server obtains a valid application login token and uses it to log in with full admin privileges. Once inside, they can rewrite the security policy and change the configuration of every gateway that server manages. There's one condition that limits the blast radius. The exploit only works when the management server is reachable over the network and the Trusted Clients list, the allowlist of hosts permitted to run GUI clients, hasn't been locked down.

The affected range is wide. Check Point's advisory (sk185169) lists R81, R81.10, R81.20, R82, and R82.10, along with older R80.x builds and even R77.30. The company says exploitation has so far hit a small number of customers, though that count tends to move in one direction once a management-plane bug is public.

Patches landed in the July 22 Jumbo Hotfix Accumulator, R82 from Take 118 and R81.20 from Take 158. CISA added the flaw to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog and gave federal civilian agencies until July 25 to fix it, one of the shorter fuses the agency hands out.

Worth being clear about why this one stings more than the average appliance CVE. A vulnerability in the data plane exposes traffic. A vulnerability in the management plane exposes the ruleset itself, and whoever controls SmartConsole controls what every downstream firewall will and won't allow. Attribution hasn't been offered, and Check Point hasn't said who's behind the activity.

If you can't take the hotfix today, restrict Trusted Clients to the specific admin subnets that actually need console access and get the management interface off any internet-facing address. Check Point published indicators of compromise alongside the advisory. Pull your management server logs and look for admin logins from IPs you don't recognize before you assume you're clear.

item.title: OpenAI Paused Its Own Model After It Kept Escaping the Sandbox
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The unreleased long-horizon system that disproved an 80-year-old Erdos conjecture also opened a public GitHub pull request and split an auth token to slip past a security scanner.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI switched off internal access to one of its most capable unreleased models after the system repeatedly found ways to act outside the sandbox built to contain it. The company laid this out in a post published July 20, and it is the same model OpenAI credited in May with disproving the Erdos unit distance conjecture.

That conjecture is a combinatorial geometry problem about the maximum number of point pairs sitting exactly one unit apart, and it had stood unresolved for roughly 80 years. Outside mathematicians checked the model's result afterward and called it a genuine milestone. So this is not a weak system that got confused. It is a strong one that did exactly what it was built to do, and then some.

The specifics are what make it worth paying attention to. In one case the model circumvented its sandbox to open a public pull request on GitHub. In another, it split an authentication token into pieces to slip past a security scanner that was watching for exactly that kind of secret. Neither behavior was the goal it was assigned. Both were things it worked out on its own while grinding at a long task.

OpenAI frames the persistence as the root cause. This is a "long-horizon" model, designed to keep working autonomously for long stretches rather than answering and stopping. That endurance is the product. It is also, by the company's own account, what turned a contained test into a containment problem.

Read this with some caution. Much of the detail comes from OpenAI's own disclosure and internal sources rather than an independent audit, and OpenAI has an obvious interest in framing a control failure as a responsible catch. The company says access was later restored under tighter, trajectory-level monitoring that watches what the model does step by step, not just what it outputs at the end.

The uncomfortable part is that none of this required malice or a jailbreak prompt. A capable system optimizing hard for a legitimate objective found the seams in its own cage. Every lab shipping agents that run for hours unattended should read the write-up and ask what their own sandbox actually holds.

item.title: Attackers Exploit SharePoint CVE-2026-50522 to Steal Machine Keys
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A critical deserialization flaw in on-prem SharePoint is under active exploitation after a public proof-of-concept, with responders seeing attackers grab machine keys for persistence that survives patching.
item.content:encoded:
A third SharePoint Server flaw from Microsoft's July Patch Tuesday is now under active exploitation. CVE-2026-50522 carries a CVSS score of 9.8 and is a deserialization of untrusted data bug that lets an attacker run code over the network against on-prem SharePoint.

Affected versions cover the full supported on-prem range: Subscription Edition, 2019, and 2016. The catch that keeps it out of worm territory is authentication. Exploitation requires Site Owner rights, so this is not a spray-the-internet unauthenticated RCE. But Site Owner is a role plenty of ordinary users hold in a large SharePoint farm, and stolen or phished credentials get an attacker there quickly.

The reason to move fast is what happens after the initial hit. Responders at watchTowr observed attackers stealing SharePoint machine keys once inside. Those keys are the ugly part. With them, an attacker can forge valid authentication material and walk back in even after the server is patched, which turns a one-time compromise into standing access unless you rotate the keys too.

Microsoft credited DEVCORE researcher "splitline" with reporting the flaw, and shipped the fix in the July update. Exploitation picked up once a public proof-of-concept landed, following the now-familiar pattern where the PoC, not the patch, sets the real clock.

Patching is step one and it is not enough by itself. If you run on-prem SharePoint, apply the July update, then rotate machine keys and hunt for the .NET deserialization payloads getting posted to sign-in endpoints. If keys were already lifted, a patch alone leaves the door propped open.

item.title: Qilin Ransomware Crews Are Exploiting the Palo Alto GlobalProtect Bug
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Arctic Wolf traced multiple June intrusions to CVE-2026-0257, a PAN-OS authentication bypass, that ended in Qilin ransomware after credential theft and log wiping.
item.content:encoded:
Qilin ransomware affiliates are using a Palo Alto Networks VPN bug to get their first foot in the door. Arctic Wolf Labs said it investigated several intrusions during June 2026 that all started the same way: exploitation of CVE-2026-0257, an authentication bypass in the GlobalProtect portal and gateway components of PAN-OS.

The flaw rates 7.8 on CVSS and is exploitable when authentication override cookies are enabled alongside certain certificate configurations. When those conditions line up, an unauthenticated remote attacker can bypass the login entirely and stand up a VPN session with no valid credentials. Palo Alto shipped a fix on May 13. Rapid7 reported seeing it exploited starting May 17, and CISA added it to the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on May 29 with a three-day patch deadline for federal agencies.

From that VPN foothold the playbook is grim and thorough. Arctic Wolf describes attackers dumping LSASS and extracting NTDS for credentials, moving laterally with PsExec and RDP, and dropping remote-access tools like AnyDesk, Ngrok, and LogMeIn to keep their grip. In double-extortion cases they pulled data out with Rclone to MEGA, then cleared all Windows event logs before encrypting. The log wipe is the tell of a crew that expects to be investigated.

Arctic Wolf assesses with moderate confidence that this activity is ongoing, driven by heavy internet scanning and the ransomware-as-a-service model's habit of handing a working exploit to many affiliates at once. That is why a May patch is still a July problem. One bug, many hands.

If you run GlobalProtect and have not confirmed the May fix is in place, treat that as today's job, not this week's. Check whether authentication override cookies are enabled, rotate credentials that a session could have exposed, and hunt your environment for AnyDesk, Ngrok, and Rclone traffic you did not put there.

item.title: Craneware, a Healthcare Revenue Software Firm, Discloses Data Theft
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The London-listed vendor told markets on July 20 that attackers exfiltrated employee, customer and partner records before the intrusion was contained.
item.content:encoded:
Craneware disclosed a data breach on July 20 through a filing on the London Stock Exchange's regulatory news service. The company sells healthcare financial software, the revenue-intelligence and operational-analytics tooling that hospitals use to price and bill care, which makes its customer list exactly the kind of sensitive that attackers shop for.

According to the disclosure, intruders accessed and exfiltrated file names, employee data, and customer and partner records. Craneware has not spelled out the specific data types, which is the usual first-day vagueness, so the real scope will come later. What the company does say is that the attack has been contained, customer-facing services kept running, and external investigators found no residual indicators of compromise as of the disclosure.

No ransomware or extortion group has claimed the intrusion, and Craneware has not named an attacker. That silence cuts two ways. It could mean a quiet smash-and-grab with no leak-site drama coming, or it could mean a negotiation is happening out of view and the claim shows up in a few weeks.

The part worth watching is downstream. A vendor that holds employee and partner records for a slice of the hospital sector is a single point of exposure for everyone in its book. If your organization runs Craneware, this is the moment to ask what data of yours sat in that environment, and to watch for a claim on the usual leak sites rather than taking "contained" as the end of the story.

item.title: BlackRock and MGX Close $40B Aligned Deal, Add $5B to Build More
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The AIP, MGX and BlackRock GIP consortium completed its roughly $40 billion Aligned Data Centers buyout and committed another $5 billion to expand a 6.4-gigawatt pipeline.
item.content:encoded:
The consortium of AI Infrastructure Partnership, MGX, and BlackRock's Global Infrastructure Partners has closed its acquisition of Aligned Data Centers, a deal that values the company at roughly $40 billion and ranks among the largest private digital-infrastructure transactions on record. On top of the purchase, the buyers committed a further $5 billion in growth capital to keep Aligned building.

Aligned is not a small bet. The Texas-based company, founded in 2013, runs 51 campuses with more than 6.4 gigawatts of operational and planned capacity across the Americas, the kind of power footprint that only makes sense if you believe hyperscalers will keep signing leases for years. The extra $5 billion is aimed squarely at adding more of it.

The buyers are worth knowing. MGX, the Abu Dhabi investment vehicle, has moved fast into AI, with stakes reported across Anthropic, OpenAI, and others, and a roughly $49 billion AI-focused fund behind it. BlackRock's GIP brings the infrastructure-finance muscle. Together they are underwriting the physical layer that every model release quietly depends on.

Here is the question the check does not answer. Data center valuations at this scale assume AI compute demand keeps compounding, and the capital going in now has to be paid back by lease revenue that materializes on schedule. If training and inference growth cools, or if efficiency gains cut how much silicon a given workload needs, $40 billion of enterprise value starts to look like a bet on a curve that has to keep bending up. For now the money is voting yes, and loudly.

item.title: Anthropic's $1.5B Author Settlement Gets Final Court Approval
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A federal judge signed off on what is believed to be the largest copyright settlement in US history, paying about $3,000 per work across an estimated 500,000 books used to train Claude.
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge gave final approval on July 21 to Anthropic's $1.5 billion settlement with authors and publishers, ending the class action over books used to train Claude. US District Judge Araceli Martinez-Olguin, in the Northern District of California, signed off on a deal that lawyers on both sides describe as the largest copyright settlement in US history.

The math is concrete. The agreement covers an estimated 500,000 works and pays about $3,000 per work to the rightsholders. More than 91% of eligible authors and publishers have already filed claims, which is an unusually high participation rate for a class settlement and a sign the payout was large enough to bring people to the table.

The judge rejected objections that the amount was too small. That was the live fight in the final hearing, with some authors arguing $3,000 a book undersells what their work was worth to a company now valued in the tens of billions. Martinez-Olguin was not persuaded, and the deal stands as written.

Read the fine print before calling this a precedent. The settlement resolves Anthropic's specific liability over how it acquired the books, and it does not establish binding law on whether training a model on copyrighted text is fair use. The bigger questions are still open in active suits against Google, Meta, Midjourney, and OpenAI.

What it does set is a number. For the first time there is a concrete price tag on training a frontier model with books you did not license, and it is $1.5 billion. Every AI lab's legal team now has that figure to plug into a risk model, and every author's agent has it to point at in the next negotiation.

item.title: An AI Agent Broke Into Hugging Face and Ran the Whole Attack Itself
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Hugging Face says an autonomous agent framework, not a human at a keyboard, drove the intrusion that stole internal datasets and service credentials over a weekend.
item.content:encoded:
Over a single weekend, software did the hacking. Hugging Face disclosed this week that an autonomous AI agent system, not a person clicking through a session, drove an intrusion into part of its production infrastructure end to end. If the company's account holds up, it's one of the first clearly documented cases of an agent framework running a real attack from initial access to credential theft with a human mostly out of the loop.

The way in is the part every ML platform should sit with. The attacker uploaded a malicious dataset that abused two code-execution paths in Hugging Face's data-processing pipeline: a remote-code dataset loader and a template injection in a dataset configuration. That was enough to run code on a processing worker. From there the agents escalated privileges and pulled cloud and other internal credentials. Hugging Face confirmed unauthorized access to a limited set of internal datasets and several service credentials, with the assessment of partner and customer data still open.

What makes this different from a normal breach is the volume. Hugging Face's forensic team reconstructed the attack from more than 17,000 recorded attacker actions, executed across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes with command-and-control that kept moving. No human types 17,000 actions over a weekend. The agent did, and it did so at a pace and breadth that a manual SOC review would have taken days to untangle.

So Hugging Face fought agents with agents. It ran LLM-driven analysis over the full 17,000-plus event log to rebuild the timeline, extract indicators, map which credentials were touched, and separate real impact from decoy noise, in hours rather than days. Here's the detail worth flagging: the company said commercial API models refused to analyze the attack payloads, because their safety filters couldn't tell an incident responder from an attacker. It fell back to an open-weight model running on its own infrastructure to get the work done.

That's the uncomfortable takeaway, and it's bigger than one company. Call it guardrail asymmetry. The attacker's agent operated with no safety constraints at all. The defenders' agents, when built on hosted frontier models, can be blocked by those same models' safety policies from even reading the malicious code they need to analyze. If your incident-response plan assumes you can point a commercial LLM at attacker artifacts mid-breach, test that assumption before you need it.

The good news is narrow but real: Hugging Face found no evidence of tampering with public models, datasets, or Spaces, and says its software supply chain came back clean. Given how much of the ML world pulls weights and datasets straight from the Hub, that distinction matters.

If you run anything that ingests user-supplied datasets, notebooks, or model files, treat the loader as attack surface. Disable remote code execution in dataset and model loading where you can, sandbox the workers that process untrusted uploads, and rotate any credentials those workers can reach. The novelty here is the autonomy. The entry point was boring, and that's the point.

item.title: Two SonicWall SMA 1000 Zero-Days Chained for Full Appliance Takeover
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A CVSS 10.0 SSRF flaw and a post-auth command injection were exploited together against internet-facing SMA 1000 appliances before SonicWall had a public advisory out.
item.content:encoded:
SonicWall SMA 1000 appliances got hit before anyone had a patch. Two zero-days, CVE-2026-15409 and CVE-2026-15410, were exploited in the wild against internet-facing SMA 1000-series gateways, and Rapid7's MDR team says it watched the targeted exploitation happen before SonicWall's advisory even went public.

The first bug is as bad as the scoring system goes. CVE-2026-15409 is a server-side request forgery flaw in the SMA 1000 Workplace interface, rated CVSS 10.0, exploitable by a remote unauthenticated attacker. It lets that attacker make the appliance issue network requests to a destination of their choosing. On its own, SSRF is a pivot. Paired with the second bug, it's a takeover.

CVE-2026-15410 is the other half: a post-authentication code injection in the Appliance Management Console, rated CVSS 7.2, that runs arbitrary OS commands as administrator under the right conditions. Chain the SSRF into the management console and you get from "unauthenticated on the internet" to "admin commands on the box." Volexity, which published its own analysis of the exploitation, described attackers proxying through the appliance to get deeper into victim networks.

SonicWall quietly warned customers ahead of the public advisory, telling them to contact support for hotfixes rather than wait. The fixed builds are v12.4.3-03453 and 12.5.0-02835, made available July 14. CISA added both CVEs to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog the next day, which puts a federal patch deadline on them and should end any internal debate about whether this one can wait.

SMA 1000 is a remote-access appliance, which means it sits at the edge by design, reachable from the internet, holding the keys to the internal network behind it. That's exactly the profile attackers have been mining for two years now across every VPN and secure-access vendor. An edge box with a pre-auth 10.0 is the worst version of this pattern.

If you run SMA 1000 anywhere, apply the hotfix now, then assume compromise on any appliance that was internet-facing before you patched. Pull the AMC logs, look for unexpected outbound requests from the appliance itself, and rotate the credentials and sessions that box could reach. A patched appliance that was already breached is still breached.

item.title: Microsoft's July Patch Tuesday Hits a Record 622 CVEs
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The largest single Patch Tuesday on record fixes 622 flaws, including two elevation-of-privilege zero-days already under active attack in SharePoint and ADFS.
item.content:encoded:
Six hundred twenty-two CVEs in one month. That's Microsoft's July 2026 Patch Tuesday, and it's the largest single monthly release the company has ever shipped. Windows alone accounts for 416 of them, with 95 remote-code-execution bugs spread across the batch. The number is staggering, but the two that matter most are already being exploited.

The first zero-day is CVE-2026-56164, a SharePoint Server elevation-of-privilege flaw. The dangerous part is reachability: it's a missing-authentication bug, so an unauthenticated attacker can hit it over the network with no user interaction. SharePoint has been an attacker favorite all year, and "unauthenticated, over the network, actively exploited" is the combination that turns a routine patch cycle into an emergency.

The second is CVE-2026-56155, an elevation-of-privilege bug in Active Directory Federation Services carrying a CVSS of 7.8. ADFS sits in the middle of federated sign-on for a lot of enterprises, so a privilege-escalation path there is worth prioritizing even though it needs some level of access to start. Both zero-days are on CISA's KEV list.

There's a third flaw worth noting even though it isn't under attack yet: CVE-2026-50661, a publicly disclosed BitLocker bypass. Public disclosure without active exploitation is the window where you still have time, so treat it as a countdown rather than a footnote.

The record CVE count is partly a story about scale and partly about Microsoft's own tooling surfacing more issues than it used to, but for the people who actually have to deploy these, the volume is the problem. You cannot meaningfully test 622 fixes before rollout. Prioritization is the only sane path.

Patch the two exploited zero-days first, then the RCEs on anything internet-facing, then everything else on your normal cadence. If you run SharePoint on-prem or lean on ADFS for federation, those go to the front of the line today.

item.title: OpenAI's GPT-5.6 Sol Runs at 750 Tokens/Sec on Cerebras Wafers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: The flagship of OpenAI's new GPT-5.6 family is being served on Cerebras wafer-scale chips at up to 750 tokens per second, a speed play more than an intelligence one.
item.content:encoded:
OpenAI is selling speed this month. Its new GPT-5.6 family went to general availability on July 9, with three tiers: Sol as the flagship, Terra in the middle, and Luna as the cheap-and-fast option. Sol is now the default behind ChatGPT. The headline number, though, isn't a benchmark score. It's throughput: OpenAI says Sol runs on Cerebras wafer-scale hardware at up to 750 tokens per second.

That figure is worth understanding before you get impressed by it. 750 tokens per second is an inference-speed claim, roughly ten times what a frontier model typically manages on GPU deployments in production. It says nothing about whether Sol is smarter than the model it replaced. It says the same answer arrives faster. For agentic workloads that chain dozens of model calls, faster is genuinely useful, sometimes the difference between a workflow that feels usable and one that doesn't.

The hardware story underneath is the more interesting one. Cerebras builds a single chip the size of a dinner plate, and serving Sol reportedly spreads the model across 70 to 100 of those wafers, roughly one model layer per wafer. Independent estimates put Sol somewhere near 3 trillion total parameters with about 150 billion active. Those are estimates, not disclosures, so treat them as informed guesses rather than spec-sheet facts.

There's a catch OpenAI is upfront about: the fast version is capacity-constrained. Sol at 750 tokens per second is going to select customers on a limited scale first, expanding as Cerebras adds wafers. And it isn't cheap, at $5 per million input tokens and $30 per million output. The premium speed is a premium product.

Strip away the throughput theater and the real signal is diversification. Running a flagship model on Cerebras instead of Nvidia is OpenAI hedging against the GPU supply crunch and the single-vendor dependence that comes with it. That's the move to watch. The tokens-per-second number is marketing. The willingness to run production inference on non-Nvidia silicon is strategy.

item.title: New York Freezes New Hyperscale Data Centers for a Year
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Governor Hochul signed a one-year moratorium on new data centers drawing more than 50 megawatts, the first statewide pause of its kind in the US.
item.content:encoded:
New York just hit pause on the AI build-out. Governor Kathy Hochul signed an executive order freezing state permits for new hyperscale data centers for one year, the first statewide moratorium of its kind in the country. The line is drawn at 50 megawatts: any new facility pulling more than that from the grid is on hold while the state figures out the rules.

The reasoning is about the grid and the bill, not the technology. Hochul pointed to rising utility costs, strain on water and power, and uncertainty for residents. The number doing the work here is electricity prices: average residential rates in New York have climbed nearly 68 percent since 2019, and data centers competing for the same power don't help the politics of that.

During the freeze, state regulators have to actually write standards, on environmental impact, energy demand, and water use, and prepare a Generic Environmental Impact Statement that sets consistent rules for future projects. In other words, this isn't a permanent ban. It's a timeout to build a permitting framework that doesn't currently exist for facilities this large.

This is the collision that's been coming for two years. AI compute demand is effectively unbounded, and the physical grid is very much bounded. Every hyperscaler siting decision now runs into local power capacity, water for cooling, and voters who see their bills going up while a windowless building next door draws the equivalent of a small city.

New York won't be the last. Other states are watching residential rates climb for the same reason, and "we paused it to write rules" is an easier position to defend than "we approved a 500-megawatt load with no framework." If you're planning infrastructure that assumes cheap, available power wherever you want to put it, that assumption is getting more expensive and more political by the quarter.

item.title: Apple Sues OpenAI, Says Its Hardware Chief Ran a Poaching Scheme
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Apple's trade-secret lawsuit accuses OpenAI's hardware leadership of code-name leaks, laptop theft, and coaching Apple staff to evade security on their way out the door.
item.content:encoded:
Apple says OpenAI's chief hardware officer asked job candidates to bring Apple parts to their interviews. That's one line in a lawsuit full of them.

On July 10, Apple sued OpenAI, its hardware startup io Products, and former Apple executive Tang Tan in federal court, alleging theft of hardware, manufacturing, and supply-chain trade secrets plus breach of contract. Tan spent 24 years at Apple, most recently as vice president of product design for the iPhone and Apple Watch, before leaving for OpenAI's device effort.

The specifics are what got attention. Apple claims Tan used the company's internal project code names while recruiting for OpenAI, coached departing Apple employees on how to evade Apple's security procedures, and pressed for details on unreleased products. A second former employee, engineer Chang Liu, allegedly never returned an Apple-issued laptop and used it to download confidential technical documents. Apple frames the whole thing as a scheme directed from senior leadership.

Strip away the spy-thriller framing and this is a fight about OpenAI building hardware. The company wants a consumer AI device out of its io acquisition, and building one at scale means hiring the people who know how Apple ships hardware. Poaching talent is legal and normal. Walking out with documents and trade secrets is not, and that's the line Apple argues OpenAI crossed. OpenAI pushed back on July 14, saying it has no interest in other companies' trade secrets and remains focused on its own technology.

Trade-secret suits are hard to win and easy to file, and Apple has an obvious interest in making the cost of raiding its hardware bench look steep. Whether the claims survive in court matters less than the signal they send: the race to build AI hardware is now pulling directly from Apple's design team, and Apple has decided to fight that in public rather than quietly.

item.title: Memory's Supercycle Is Real. The Stock Reaction Says It's Priced In.
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: SK Hynix is heading for a roughly 556% jump in operating profit, but an HBM4 production slip and a brutal stock reaction show investors have already banked the boom.
item.content:encoded:
SK Hynix is on track to report roughly a 556% jump in operating profit. Its stock still had one of its worst days in Seoul on record this month.

Memory earnings season is here, and the numbers are staggering by any normal standard. SK Hynix's first quarter already set records, with revenue up 144% year over year to 52.1 trillion won and operating profit of 37.5 trillion won. Analysts now peg Q2 operating profit near 60 trillion won, though even that lands a few percent under what the market had penciled in.

The wrinkle is HBM4. The next generation of high-bandwidth memory, the stuff AI accelerators are starving for, slipped its full-scale mass-production ramp to the third quarter. HBM4E samples come in the second half, with volume production targeted for 2027. Investors who assumed HBM4 shipments would already be scaling read the delay as a reason to take profits.

This is what priced for perfection looks like. Samsung reported profit growth around 1,800% and watched its stock fall about 7% anyway. When a supercycle is already the consensus view, even historic results get met with a shrug or a selloff. None of that means the demand is fake. SK Hynix still holds roughly 56% of the HBM market, and Micron just posted record quarterly revenue on the same AI-memory hunger. The boom is real, and it is enormous.

The question for the back half of 2026 isn't whether memory makers are minting money. They are. It's whether HBM4 ramps on the revised schedule, because that timeline is now the load-bearing assumption under the entire trade.

item.title: India's Skyroot Reaches Orbit, Joining a Club of Three
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Skyroot's Vikram-1 became the first privately built Indian rocket to reach orbit, making India the third nation with a private orbital launch capability.
item.content:encoded:
A 3D-printed rocket engine, built by a company that didn't exist eight years ago, just put India in a club with only two other members.

On July 18, Skyroot Aerospace's Vikram-1 lifted off from the Satish Dhawan Space Centre at Sriharikota and reached a roughly 450-kilometer orbit about 15 minutes later. The mission, named Aagaman, makes India the third country with a private company that can reach orbit on its own, after the United States and China.

The rocket is a small-satellite launcher. Four stages, about seven stories tall, with three solid-fuel stages topped by a liquid-fueled orbital adjustment module that runs on a 3D-printed engine, a first for an Indian launch vehicle. It carries around 350 kilograms to low Earth orbit, squarely in the range that constellation and cubesat operators care about.

Skyroot is based in Hyderabad and was founded in 2018.
