It became the first Indian space startup to reach a $1 billion valuation earlier this year, and this flight is the payoff from six years of policy reform that opened orbital launch to private builders working alongside ISRO. India spent decades with launch as a government monopoly. Now it has a commercial one that works.

The small-sat launch market is crowded and unforgiving on margins, and a single successful debut doesn't make a viable business. But a private Indian rocket in orbit changes who gets to bid for that market, and at what price. That's the part worth watching.

item.title: CitrixBleed Is Back: NetScaler Memory Bug Exploited in Under a Day
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A pre-auth memory overread in NetScaler's SAML handling, CVE-2026-8451, was under active exploitation less than 24 hours after Citrix patched it.
item.content:encoded:
Citrix shipped the patch on June 30. Attackers were exploiting the hole in under 24 hours.

CVE-2026-8451 is one of six NetScaler ADC and Gateway flaws Citrix fixed that day. It's a pre-authentication memory overread, rated CVSS 8.8, in the XML parser NetScaler uses when it's configured as a SAML identity provider. No credentials required. An attacker sends a crafted request, forces the appliance to read past its buffer, and gets chunks of process memory handed back inside an HTTP response cookie.

The name isn't marketing. This is the same class of bug as CitrixBleed, the 2023 flaw that leaked session tokens and let attackers ride authenticated sessions straight past multi-factor auth. The root cause this time is small and ugly: the parser didn't terminate unquoted XML attribute values when a newline followed, so it kept reading into whatever was next in memory.

Researchers at watchTowr published a technical writeup the same day Citrix disclosed, and honeypot sensors recorded a working exploit within a roughly five-hour window spanning June 30 into July 1. That's the pattern now. When a memory-disclosure bug in an internet-facing VPN appliance gets full technical detail on day one, the window to mass exploitation is measured in hours, not weeks.

Patch to the fixed NetScaler builds if you haven't. And if your appliance ran as a SAML IdP while exposed to the internet, patching alone won't save you. Rotate session secrets and terminate active sessions, because anything that leaked out of memory, tokens included, is already gone. CitrixBleed taught this exact lesson in 2023. The sequel has the same plot.

item.title: EY Says Client Tax Files Stolen Through a Third-Party Help Desk
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Ernst & Young disclosed that attackers accessed a third-party IT support platform and downloaded client tax documents, including Social Security numbers and investment holdings.
item.content:encoded:
The data in an accountant's support ticket is exactly the data a criminal wants: Social Security numbers, bank account codes, investment holdings, and the actual contents of people's tax filings. Ernst & Young just confirmed a batch of it walked out the door.

EY, one of the Big Four, disclosed that an unauthorized party got into a third-party IT service management platform its staff used to support client tax work. The attackers had access from March 28 to April 12, and downloaded client documents during that window. EY spotted suspicious activity on April 23, filed a breach notification with California's Attorney General on July 15, and has notified at least four states.

That's roughly a three-week gap between the intrusion and detection, and the stolen material is about as sensitive as personal data gets. According to the disclosures, it included Social Security numbers, financial account and routing codes, credit and debit account data, investment holdings, and the contents of client tax returns.

EY hasn't named a threat actor or said whether ransomware was involved. What it has confirmed is the shape of the attack, and it's a familiar one in 2026: not EY's own network, but a vendor platform holding EY's data. The help-desk tool you trust with support tickets becomes the soft path to your clients' most sensitive records.

EY is offering affected people 24 months of identity monitoring through Experian. If you're an EY tax client, don't wait on the letter. Assume the data is out, freeze your credit, and be ready for tax-fraud attempts and phishing that quotes real details from your filings to sound legitimate. Monitoring after the fact tells you when someone uses your data. It doesn't stop them.

item.title: An AI Agent Broke Into Hugging Face and Logged 17,000 Actions
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Hugging Face says an autonomous AI agent breached its production infrastructure through a malicious dataset, harvested internal credentials, and ran end to end with no human at the keyboard.
item.content:encoded:
Seventeen thousand actions. That's how many moves an autonomous AI agent made inside Hugging Face's production infrastructure before the company pieced together what it had done.

In a disclosure published July 20, the world's largest AI model repository described an intrusion unlike anything it had handled before. It wasn't a person with a keyboard. It was an autonomous agent framework, one that appears to have been built on an agentic security-research harness, running thousands of individual actions across a swarm of short-lived sandboxes.

The way in was a dataset. A malicious dataset abused two code-execution paths, the remote-code dataset loader and a template injection in a dataset configuration, and both let attacker code run on a data-processing worker. From that worker the agent got node-level access, then harvested cloud and cluster credentials and moved laterally across internal clusters over a weekend.

There is good news buried in the report. Hugging Face found no tampering with public, user-facing models, datasets, or Spaces, and it verified that container images and published packages were clean. The software supply chain held. The internal-cluster access is the part that should keep people up at night.

The sharpest detail is about the defense. To reconstruct more than 17,000 events, Hugging Face ran its own LLM analysis agents over the attacker log. When it tried to use frontier model APIs for parts of that work, the models' safety guardrails balked at analyzing the attacker's actions, so the team fell back to a self-hosted open-weight model (GLM 5.2) on internal infrastructure and finished in hours. The attacker had no such guardrails. If your incident-response plan depends on a model that might refuse the job, you don't have an incident-response plan.

The practical takeaway is old advice with new urgency. If you run pipelines that load untrusted datasets or render configs, treat those loaders and template paths as remote code execution surfaces: sandbox them hard and scope worker credentials to the minimum. The novelty here isn't the entry point. It's that the whole intrusion ran at machine speed with nobody steering it.

item.title: Starship's Flight 13 Aborts at T-0 After Four Engines Refuse to Light
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: SpaceX scrubbed Starship's 13th test flight a second before liftoff when four Raptor engines failed to ignite, triggering an automatic shutdown of the rest.
item.content:encoded:
Starship came within about a second of leaving the pad on Thursday, then didn't. Four of its 33 Raptor engines failed to ignite during the startup sequence, and the flight computer did exactly what it's supposed to do: it shut the other 29 down and kept the rocket bolted to the ground, wrapped in smoke and vapor.

This was a first. For all the drama of earlier Starship tests, a full-scale vehicle had never triggered a last-second abort at T-0 like this. The automatic shutdown is the system working, not failing. Catching a bad ignition and standing down beats lifting off on 29 of 33 engines and finding out what happens next over the Gulf.

Elon Musk said on X that two engines will be swapped out before the next attempt, and that the most probable launch window is early next week. At 407 feet with 33 main engines, Starship is the largest and most powerful rocket ever built, and getting all 33 to light in the right fraction of a second is exactly the kind of problem that doesn't fully show up until you're doing it for real.

There's a NASA deadline hanging over this. Starship is the lander for returning astronauts to the Moon, and the program's schedule leans on these test flights going well and going soon. A scrub isn't a setback in engineering terms. It is one in calendar terms, and the calendar is the part NASA cares about.

The retarget lands on July 20 if the window holds, which is a nice bit of timing. Apollo 11 touched down on the Moon on July 20, 1969. Watch the ignition sequence on the next attempt. That one second is where this flight lives or dies.

item.title: Report: US Pressed Samsung and SK Hynix to Share AI 'Excess Profits'
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Korean press reports say a US trade official told Seoul that Washington has a right to share in the memory-chip windfall driven by the AI boom, a claim the US has not confirmed.
item.content:encoded:
Washington reportedly wants a cut of the money South Korea's memory-chip makers are pulling in off the AI boom. According to reports out of Seoul, a US trade official told his Korean counterpart that the US has a right to share in the "excess profits" of Samsung Electronics and SK Hynix.

The claim traces to a meeting in which Deputy US Trade Representative Rick Switzer reportedly raised the idea with Korea's trade minister. It has not been officially confirmed by the US side. The backdrop is real enough: South Korean semiconductor exports to the US jumped more than 90% year over year in the first half of 2026, and both companies sell the high-bandwidth memory that AI accelerators depend on.

The numbers behind the demand are eye-catching, and worth a grain of salt. Reports cite projections of a massive jump in Samsung's 2026 profit and an even steeper climb for SK Hynix off a small 2025 base. These are forecasts, not booked results, so read them as the shape of the windfall rather than a settled figure.

A foreign government asking to share in a private company's profits is unusual and legally murky. Korea's trade ministry said it was unaware of any such request. This reads less like a concrete policy and more like an opening position in a wider negotiation over tariffs and US investment commitments, the kind of maximalist ask that gets floated to see what sticks.

If any of it is confirmed on the record, it's a new way of tying chip revenue to trade leverage. For now it's a report, and the thing to watch is whether either government says the words out loud.

item.title: Anthropic May Rent $10 Billion of Compute From a Direct Rival, Meta
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Anthropic is in early talks to lease up to $10 billion in data-center capacity from Meta, whose Llama models compete head-on with Claude.
item.content:encoded:
Anthropic is in early talks to rent up to $10 billion in computing capacity from Meta. That's the same Meta that builds the Llama models competing directly with Claude. Reuters and the New York Times reported the discussions this week.

The terms are preliminary. The talks reportedly began in June on a proposal from Anthropic, with payments made in monthly increments over roughly two years, and either side can walk away before anything is signed. Nothing is final, and "up to $10 billion" is a ceiling, not a check that's been written.

What makes this odd is the shape of it. Meta ships its own frontier models and would, under this arrangement, also become the landlord renting Anthropic the infrastructure to train and serve a rival. The logic on Meta's side is that hyperscalers have spent enormously on data centers, and leasing out spare capacity turns some of that capex into a revenue line. On Anthropic's side, it's about getting enough compute, from wherever it can, fast enough to keep up.

Anthropic already leans on Amazon and Google for capacity. Adding Meta would be less about strategy and more about raw availability, which is the tell. When a company is willing to buy compute from a direct competitor, scarcity has clearly started to outweigh the awkwardness.

Early-stage deals leak for a reason, so treat the number as a headline, not a done deal. If it does close, the signal matters more than the dollar figure: the fight for compute has gotten intense enough that rivals will do business with each other to get it.

item.title: Microsoft's 'Project Perception' Takes Aim at Anthropic's Mythos Bug Hunter
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Microsoft is reportedly readying an AI security product that finds and fixes software bugs across code, cloud, and endpoints, priced to undercut Anthropic's Mythos.
item.content:encoded:
Microsoft wants to find your software bugs with AI, fix them automatically, and charge less than Anthropic to do it. The company is preparing to launch a security product internally codenamed Project Perception, according to a report from The Information, and it's built to look across a company's code, cloud infrastructure, and endpoints, flag exploitable weaknesses, explain the impact, and propose concrete fixes.

The interesting piece is how it's wired. Rather than betting on a single model, Perception reportedly uses a router that picks the best model per task, drawing on Microsoft's own models plus ones from OpenAI and Anthropic. It ties into the security estate Microsoft already sells: Defender XDR for endpoint signals, Defender for Cloud, Entra ID for identity, and GitHub for source. The pitch is that combining those inputs answers questions a standalone scanner can't.

The target is obvious. Anthropic's Mythos does autonomous bug-finding and patching, and it's expensive to run. Reporting puts Mythos API costs well above both Opus and GPT pricing, and Microsoft's per-task routing is the lever it plans to pull to come in cheaper. Cheap enough, the framing goes, to run continuously instead of in occasional audits.

Skepticism is the right default on the AI security beat. This is still a report about an unshipped product that's supposedly launching "as soon as this month." AI bug-finders are genuinely useful and also genuinely oversold. The hard part was never generating a list of candidate bugs. It's the false-positive rate, and whether an auto-proposed fix is safe to actually merge without a human who understands the codebase signing off.

Cost routing helps adoption. It says nothing about accuracy. For Windows-heavy shops already living inside Defender and Entra, the real moat isn't the model, it's the integration, and no competitor can replicate the telemetry Microsoft already holds. The number worth waiting for is the false-positive rate when this ships. Everything else is a demo.

item.title: Ecopetrol Blocked the Encryption, But Attackers Still Walked Out With Data
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Colombia's largest company stopped a ransomware payload from firing, yet an intruder still downloaded data tied to about 3,300 accounts and is now demanding money.
item.content:encoded:
The ransomware didn't fire. That's the unusual part.

Ecopetrol, Colombia's state-controlled oil producer and the country's biggest company, said an intruder reached its cloud file storage on July 17 and tried to launch ransomware. The encryption never ran. Company controls caught and blocked it before it could lock any systems, and Ecopetrol reported no material disruption to production or critical operations.

The attacker still got something. Data tied to roughly 3,300 user accounts, spread across about 15 subsidiaries, was downloaded before the intrusion was contained. The company revoked the unauthorized access, blocked the mass-download mechanisms, and disclosed the incident publicly. The actor, so far unidentified, has since made an extortion demand, threatening to publish the stolen data. As of Ecopetrol's latest statement, nothing has surfaced on leak sites.

Most breach disclosures we cover are about the encryption that did fire, the plant that went dark, the hospital diverting ambulances. This one is the more common and less dramatic middle outcome: execution blocked, data gone anyway. It's worth paying attention to precisely because the controls worked as designed on the part that would have made headlines.

Still, "contained" is carrying a lot of weight here. The data already left the building, and the leverage now is publication, not encryption. "No evidence of publication" is a snapshot, not a promise. On the other side, 3,300 accounts is a small number for a company this size, which suggests either tight segmentation held or the attacker simply didn't get far before being cut off.

The tell to watch is whether the data shows up on an extortion leak site in the coming weeks. If it does, the story shifts from a blocked attack to a slow-motion data breach.

item.title: CISA Sets Today's Deadline for FortiSandbox Flaws Under Active Attack
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Two unauthenticated command-injection bugs in Fortinet's malware sandbox are being exploited now, and federal agencies have until July 19 to patch.
item.content:encoded:
The appliance that's supposed to catch malware is now a way in. CISA has ordered federal agencies to patch two FortiSandbox flaws by today, July 19, after confirming both are being used in real attacks.

The bugs are CVE-2026-39808 and CVE-2026-25089, both OS command injection (CWE-78). An unauthenticated attacker sends a crafted HTTP request and runs arbitrary operating-system commands on the box, no credentials required. CVE-2026-39808 hits FortiSandbox directly. CVE-2026-25089 has the wider blast radius, reaching FortiSandbox, FortiSandbox Cloud, and FortiSandbox PaaS. CISA added both to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog on July 16 under Binding Operational Directive 26-04.

FortiSandbox isn't a corner appliance. It detonates suspicious files, which means it's wired into email gateways, endpoints, and file shares, and it usually runs with high privilege so it can inspect anything you throw at it. Handing an unauthenticated attacker command execution on a box with that much reach is close to a worst case.

This keeps happening to edge security gear. Fortinet, Ivanti, SonicWall: the devices sitting at the network boundary, the ones meant to keep attackers out, have become the reliable way in. A sandbox getting popped by the very traffic it's built to analyze is the same story with a sharper edge.

Check FortiGuard's PSIRT advisory for the exact fixed builds and update now. If your FortiSandbox management interface has been reachable from the internet, don't assume you're clean because you patched today. Treat it as potentially compromised, pull logs, and hunt for unexpected commands or new accounts. The federal deadline is federal, but the exploitation is everyone's problem.

item.title: Gemini 3.5 Pro Slips Months as DeepMind Loses Four Researchers
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Google's flagship model is months behind after missing internal coding targets, and four senior DeepMind researchers left in a single week.
item.content:encoded:
Google's next flagship model isn't ready, and the reason is the one thing developers care about most: coding.

Gemini 3.5 Pro is months behind schedule. Google refreshed its training data late in June specifically to sharpen coding performance, and the results still weren't good enough to ship. The model remains in limited preview for select Vertex AI enterprise customers, with general availability now targeted for sometime in July.

The delay landed the same week as a talent bleed. Four senior DeepMind researchers left in a matter of days: Gemini co-lead Noam Shazeer to OpenAI, Nobel laureate John Jumper to Anthropic, and researchers Jonas Adler and Alexander Pritzel also to Anthropic. Losing your model's co-lead and a Nobel winner in the same week isn't a coincidence you wave off.

Google's problem isn't raw model quality on a benchmark sheet. It's that the company lacks a credible commercial coding product while OpenAI, Anthropic, and a wave of startups have shipped agents developers actually use. DeepMind staff have reportedly flagged this internally. Meanwhile Google Cloud, DeepMind, Android, and consumer teams have each built their own AI coding tools, competing for the same people and budget.

Investors noticed. The delay and the departures helped wipe roughly $225 billion off Alphabet's market cap. That's a large number for a model that will still ship eventually, which tells you the market is pricing the org chart as much as the release date.

A delayed model is recoverable. A pattern of your best researchers choosing competitors is harder to fix, because it compounds. The real question for Google isn't whether Gemini 3.5 Pro eventually ships. It's whether the people who'd build 4.0 are still in the building.

item.title: Chip Stocks Sell Off Hard Even as Earnings Come In Strong
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: A tech-led selloff dragged the Nasdaq down more than 1% on July 17, with chipmakers falling despite TSMC and ASML both beating expectations.
item.content:encoded:
TSMC posted record profit. ASML raised its forecast. And chip stocks fell anyway.

On July 17 the Nasdaq dropped about 1.4%, the S&P 500 lost roughly 1%, and semiconductors led the way down. What makes the selloff notable is the timing: it landed in the same week as two blowout earnings reports from companies sitting at the center of the AI buildout.

When good news stops pushing a stock up, that's the market telling you the good news was already priced in. Chip names have run for the better part of two years on AI demand. A quarter of strong results that fails to spark a rally looks less like a verdict on the businesses and more like fatigue with the valuations.

None of this says the AI buildout is slowing. TSMC's own numbers point the other way. What's wobbling is the share price, not the demand, and those are different things that headlines love to blur together. Profit-taking after a long run is ordinary. It only becomes a story when it happens on a day that by all rights should have been green.

Worth watching whether this is a one-day wobble or the start of a real repricing. The tell will be the next round of earnings from the buyers of chips, not the sellers. If the hyperscalers keep guiding capital spending higher, the demand story holds regardless of what the tape does this week.

item.title: Intel Is First to Ship High-Volume Chips Made With High-NA EUV
item.author: noreply@sabr-labs.com (Sam Browand)
item.description: Select layers of Intel's 18A Panther Lake chips are now being mass-produced on ASML's newest lithography tools, a first for the industry.
item.content:encoded:
For the first time, commercial logic chips are shipping to customers with layers printed by ASML's High-NA EUV machines. Intel got there first.

ASML confirmed the milestone on July 15. Intel has qualified High-NA (the 0.55 numerical aperture generation of extreme ultraviolet lithography) for selected layers of its 18A process in Oregon, and is using it to build parts of the Core Ultra Series 3 "Panther Lake" processors. Those layers are dual-qualified, meaning they can run on both the new 0.55 NA scanners and the older 0.33 NA ones, at yields Intel says match its existing platform.

High-NA tools run around $400 million each and print finer features in a single exposure, which can replace the slow, yield-hungry multi-pass patterning older tools need. Getting one into high-volume production is the genuinely hard part. TSMC and Samsung own these machines too. Intel shipping product first is a real bragging right for a foundry that's spent years playing catch-up.

"Selected layers" is carrying weight in that sentence. This isn't a chip built end to end on High-NA. It's a handful of critical layers where the tool earns its cost, with the rest still on 0.33 NA. That's the normal way a new lithography generation enters production, and it's real progress. It's also not a full-node transition, so the "Intel leapfrogs everyone" read is premature.

The numbers that matter next are yield at scale and whether Intel Foundry can turn this into external customer wins. A first-shipment headline is good. Signed foundry contracts on 18A would be better.
